requirements.test: An affidavit whose filing or service on the opposite party is less than three days before the listed hearing is flagged unusable, and can only be used with a recorded leave order.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 46 says that except with the leave of the court no affidavit which has not been filed in court, and of which a copy has not been given to the opposite side at least three days before the hearing, shall be used in any matter; rule 83 of the High Court Rules repeats it. The bar, the period and the single exception are all in the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the date on which a copy of each affidavit was given to the opposite party, separately from the date the affidavit was filed in court.
requirements.why: The rule requires both events - filing in court, and giving a copy to the opposite side - to have happened three days before the hearing, so the usable date is the later of the two; counter-affidavits are keyed to the day the copy was given. The rule does not in terms say the two dates are to be stored separately, but a record that carries only the filing date cannot show whether the accused had the complainant's evidence in time, and every dispute about it becomes oral.

binds.target: affidavit - date copy given to the opposite party

requirements.test: The affidavit record holds a filing date and a service-on-opposite-party date as distinct populated fields, and the three-day check uses the later of them.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 46 makes both events, filing in court and giving a copy to the opposite side, conditions of using the affidavit, and rule 48 keys the right to file a counter-affidavit to the copy having been given. Neither rule says the two dates are to be held as separate fields. That they must be, because the usable date is the later of the two, is the reading taken here.

requirements.statement: The system MUST mark exhibits by the party who filed them, using the prescribed capital letter and a continuing numeral, and MUST run the numerals consecutively across exhibits marked by several accused.
requirements.why: P, D and C with running numerals is how a Kerala record is read on appeal. A system that marks exhibits by upload order, or restarts numbering per accused where the rule requires exhibits marked by several accused to run consecutively, produces a record in which the judgment's references do not resolve to the documents.

binds.target: exhibit mark

requirements.how: Prosecution exhibits P1, P2, P3; defence exhibits D1, D2, D3; court exhibits C1, C2, C3; exhibits marked by several accused numbered consecutively.
requirements.test: Mark documents for the complainant, for two separate accused and by the court; the marks take the prescribed letters and the defence numerals run consecutively across both accused rather than restarting at D1.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 62(1) fixes P, D and C with running numerals for prosecution, defence and court exhibits, and rule 62(2) says all exhibits marked by several accused shall be marked consecutively. The letters, the numerals and the rule against restarting the series for each accused are all in the sub-rules.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record that an interpreter took an oath or made an affirmation before being called upon to interpret, in the form the rules prescribe for an interpreter.
requirements.why: The interpreter's oath is a separate oath from the witness's, in different words - to well and truly interpret and explain all questions put and evidence given. Kerala's court language is Malayalam, so a bank official or an out-of-state accused giving evidence through an interpreter is ordinary in a cheque case. If the record does not show the interpreter was sworn, the evidence taken through him is open to challenge in its entirety.

binds.target: interpreter - oath or affirmation record

requirements.how: The prescribed form: to well and truly interpret and explain all questions put to and evidence given by witnesses.
requirements.test: Assigning an interpreter to an examination requires an oath record for that interpreter before evidence can be recorded in the session.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 49 requires every witness and every interpreter to take an oath or make an affirmation before he is examined or called upon to interpret, and rule 52 gives the interpreter's oath its own words. What the rules command is the act at the hearing; neither says the oath must appear in the record, or that evidence may not be taken until it does. Requiring a stored oath record as the precondition of recording evidence is a system-level consequence of the rules, which is why the status was moved off firm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record that the oath to a witness or interpreter was administered in open court by the Presiding Officer or by a person he has empowered in that behalf, or by the Commissioner where the witness is examined on commission.
requirements.why: Who administered the oath, and whether it happened in open court, are the facts that make the deposition admissible. A record that simply carries a sworn flag cannot answer a challenge that the oath was administered in chambers or by a clerk with no authority, and in a cheque trial conducted partly over video the question is a live one.

binds.target: oath - administering officer and setting

requirements.how: Administered in open court by the Presiding Officer or by such other person as he has empowered in that behalf, or, where the witness is examined on commission, by the Commissioner.
requirements.test: Every oath record names the officer who administered it and the authority under which he did so; a sworn flag with no administering officer cannot be saved.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 50 says the oath to witnesses and interpreters shall be administered in open court by the Presiding Officer or by such other person as he has empowered in that behalf, or by the Commissioner where the witness is examined on commission. The rule governs who may administer the oath and where; it does not direct that the administering officer or the setting be recorded against the deposition. Making those stored fields is the step taken here so that a challenge to the oath can be answered from the record, and it is why the status was moved off firm.

requirements.statement: Where a witness cannot understand the language in which the oath or affirmation is administered, the system MUST record that it was translated by the interpreter, put to the witness, and taken by the witness in a language known to him.
requirements.why: An oath the witness did not understand binds nobody. In Kerala the oath is put in Malayalam, so a non-Malayalam-speaking accused giving evidence, or a bank witness from outside the state, must be sworn through the interpreter and in his own language. A system that captures a single sworn flag erases the whole event and leaves the deposition's foundation unproved.

binds.target: oath - language of administration and translation

requirements.how: The oath or affirmation is translated by the interpreter and put to the witness, and the witness is allowed to take it in the language known to him.
requirements.test: Where the witness's language differs from the language of the oath, the oath record captures the translating interpreter and the language in which the oath was actually taken.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 53 directs that where the witness cannot understand the language in which the oath is administered it shall be translated by the interpreter and put to the witness, who is allowed to take it in the language known to him, and rule 51 prescribes the words. Both rules command what is to happen at the hearing and neither requires the record to capture it. Holding the translating interpreter and the language the oath was actually taken in as fields is our reading of what makes the deposition's foundation provable, so the status was moved off firm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record, in the heading of a deposition, the witness's full name including the family name, the father's, mother's or husband's name, and the age, profession and residence of the witness.
requirements.why: The deposition heading is how a witness is identified years later on appeal or in a connected case, when the same common name appears on several files. A deposition captured under a display name and a case-party role cannot be tied to a person, and where the witness is a bank officer proving the return memo, the profession and place are the very particulars that establish his competence to prove it.

binds.target: deposition - heading particulars

requirements.how: The full name including the family name of the deponent, his or her father's or mother's or husband's name, and the age, profession and residence of the witness.
requirements.test: The rendered deposition heading carries all the listed particulars, drawn from stored fields rather than free text.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 56 requires the heading of a deposition to record the full name including the family name of the deponent, the father's or mother's or husband's name, and the age, profession and residence of the witness. Every particular the requirement names is in the rule, and the rule is addressed to the document rather than to the event.

requirements.statement: Where a witness is examined through an interpreter, the system MUST print the interpreter's name in the deposition heading, below the witness's particulars.
requirements.why: Kerala puts the interpreter on the face of the deposition because the accuracy of the evidence is only as good as the interpretation, and a challenge to the evidence is a challenge to a named person. A deposition that records the interpretation as an internal attribute leaves the appellate court unable to see, from the document, that the evidence was interpreted at all.

binds.target: deposition - interpreter named in the heading

requirements.how: The name of the interpreter, if any, written below the witness's name, age, profession and residence.
requirements.test: Assigning an interpreter to an examination causes the interpreter's name to appear in the rendered deposition heading below the witness particulars.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 56 closes by saying the name of the interpreter, if any, shall be written below the particulars stated above. Both the particular and its placement in the heading come from that sentence.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a deposition to be read over to the witness and signed in full by him on its last page, and MUST require the Judge to initial every page not recorded in his own hand.
requirements.why: A cheque trial's cross-examination is typed by a stenographer, so every page is a page not in the Judge's hand. Unless each is initialled and the witness signs the last page after the read-over, there is nothing distinguishing the record from a transcript typed afterwards, and the deposition can be disputed page by page.

binds.target: deposition - read over, signed and initialled

requirements.how: After the deposition has been read over to the witness, the last page is signed in full by him, and the Judge initials every page if the deposition is not recorded in his hand.
requirements.test: Closing a deposition requires a witness signature on the final page and a judicial initial on every page recorded by a stenographer.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 57 says that after a deposition has been read over to the witness the last page shall be signed in full by him, and that the Judge shall initial every page if the deposition is not recorded in his hand. Both marks are required on the document itself, so the requirement checks what the rule puts on the page.

requirements.statement: The system MUST append to every deposition the prescribed certificate, signed by the Judge over his name, stating whether it was taken down by him or before him and whether it was interpreted or read over to the witness and admitted by him to be correct.
requirements.why: The certificate is where the interpretation and the read-over are proved. Kerala prescribes its words, and the alternatives in it are not decorative - a deposition certified as read over when it was in fact interpreted misdescribes what happened at the hearing, and that is the first thing tested when the accused says the witness never said what the record shows.

binds.target: deposition - Judge's certificate

requirements.how: The certificate in the prescribed words, with the alternatives resolved: taken down by me or before me in open court, interpreted or read over to the witness and admitted by him to be correct, signed by the Judge over his name.
requirements.test: The rendered certificate resolves each alternative from stored facts rather than printing both, and cannot be produced without the Judge's name.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 57 prescribes the certificate to be appended at the foot of the deposition and requires the Judge to affix his signature to it over his name. The alternatives inside the prescribed words, taken down by me or before me and interpreted or read over, are the rule's own, so resolving them rather than printing both is what the rule asks for.

requirements.statement: Where a document produced with a pleading is not the original, the system MUST carry the producing advocate's or party's endorsement on the top of its first page stating that it is a certified copy or a photocopy and not the original.
requirements.why: The cheque and the bank return memo are the case. Kerala requires the party who produces a copy to say on the face of it that it is a copy, and a system that uploads scans with no such endorsement leaves the court unable to tell a scanned original from a scanned photocopy - which is exactly the confusion that lets a disputed cheque be treated as proved.

binds.target: e-filed document that is not the original - endorsement

requirements.how: Endorsed on the top of the first page by the advocate or party-in-person producing it, that the document is not the original and is only a certified copy or a photocopy.
requirements.test: Marking an uploaded document as a copy stamps the endorsement on the first page of the stored PDF; a document marked as a copy without the endorsement cannot be filed.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(6) requires the advocate or party-in-person producing a document that is not the original to endorse on the top of the first page of the document that it is not the original and is only a certified copy or a photocopy. The endorsement, its wording and its position are all in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: Where the original of an e-filed document is not clearly legible, the system MUST require a typed copy certified by the advocate or party-in-person to be scanned and uploaded alongside it.
requirements.why: A handwritten cheque, a faint bank stamp on a return memo and a carbon-copy acknowledgement of a demand notice are all routinely illegible once scanned. Kerala's answer is a certified typed copy filed with the original. Without it the Registry cannot read the cheque number or the return reason at scrutiny, and the objection comes back to the complainant days later.

binds.target: illegible original - certified typed copy

requirements.how: A typed copy of the document, duly certified by the advocate or party-in-person, scanned and uploaded along with the original.
requirements.test: Flagging an uploaded document as not clearly legible requires a second file recorded as the certified typed copy before the filing can be submitted.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(5) says that when the original of the document is not clearly legible a typed copy duly certified by the advocate or party-in-person shall also be scanned and uploaded along with the original. The trigger and the second file are both stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record, against every scanned document, the person who electronically filed it as the person responsible for producing the original when the court directs.
requirements.why: The Kerala rule puts that responsibility on the e-filer by name. When the accused disputes the cheque and the court calls for the original, the case stalls if nobody can say who holds it - and the complainant's advocate, the clerk who uploaded it and the litigant will each point at the others.

binds.target: scanned document - person responsible for the original

requirements.test: Every scanned document stores the e-filer responsible for its original, and a call for production resolves to that person.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 8(3) says the responsibility for producing the originals of the documents shall be on the person who has electronically filed the scanned copies, and rule 8(1) requires those originals to be preserved for production as and when directed by the court. The rule allocates the responsibility to a person the act of electronic filing already identifies, so the requirement only makes the record resolve to him rather than creating the duty.

requirements.statement: The system MUST number material objects in a single continuous Arabic series, whether they are exhibited for the prosecution, the defence or the court.
requirements.why: The material object series is deliberately not split by party, so that M.O. 3 identifies one thing in the case and not three. A store that numbers material objects inside each party's own sequence produces a record in which a judgment's reference to a material object is ambiguous, and the object cannot be traced through the record on appeal.

binds.target: material object number

requirements.how: All material objects marked in Arabic numbers in continuous series, whether exhibited for the prosecution or the defence or the Court, as M.O. 1, M.O. 2, M.O. 3.
requirements.test: Material objects produced by the complainant, by the accused and by the court take numbers from one shared counter, and no two objects in the case carry the same number.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 62(3) says all material objects shall be marked in Arabic numbers in continuous series, whether exhibited for the prosecution or the defence or the court. The single series across all three is the sub-rule's express point of contrast with the party-lettered exhibit marks in rule 62(1).

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT schedule or record a judicial act on a holiday unless a case of absolute urgency has been recorded.
requirements.why: Kerala's rule is that no case shall be heard and no judicial act formally announced or done on a holiday save in a case of absolute urgency. A listing engine that treats a 24x7 court as having no calendar will put a cheque case's evidence or judgment on a gazetted holiday, and the order is open to challenge for a reason that has nothing to do with its merits.

binds.target: listing - judicial acts on a holiday

requirements.test: Listing a hearing on a court holiday is blocked unless an absolute-urgency reason is recorded against it.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(2) says no case shall be heard and no judicial act shall be formally announced or done on a holiday save in case of absolute urgency, and rule 5(3) carves out the detention, lunacy, dying declaration and release functions the bar does not touch. The prohibition and its exception are both express; requiring the urgency to be recorded is only how the exception is evidenced.

requirements.statement: The system SHOULD default a court's sitting window to 11:00 to 17:00 with an interval not exceeding one hour.
requirements.why: The rule says courts shall ordinarily sit in that window, which is a default and not an absolute. A scheduler with no default will spread a cheque case's hearings across hours when nobody is sitting; one that hard-codes the window cannot express the Kollam ON Court, which is designated to run round the clock. It has to be a default that a court record can override.

binds.target: court - sitting hours and interval

requirements.how: Ordinarily from 11.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m. with an interval not exceeding one hour.
requirements.test: A newly created court inherits the 11:00 to 17:00 window and the interval cap, and the values can be overridden on the court record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 5(1) says the courts shall ordinarily sit from 11.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m. with an interval not exceeding one hour. Ordinarily is what makes it a default rather than a fixed window, which is why the level is SHOULD and why the value has to sit on the court record.

requirements.statement: Where an accused before a subordinate criminal court has been exempted from personal appearance, the system MUST require the pleader appearing for him to file a vakalatnama in the prescribed form, and MUST NOT accept a memorandum of appearance in its place.
requirements.why: Exemption from personal appearance is the ordinary course in a Kerala cheque case, and this is the rule that pairs with it: the pleader who appears for an absent accused must hold a vakalath, not merely a memo. A system that offers the memo route to every criminal accused will let a case run to judgment against an accused who never appeared and whose counsel never held a written authority.

binds.target: appearance for an exempted accused - vakalatnama required

requirements.how: A vakalath as prescribed by Rule 32, in Judicial Form No. 57.
requirements.test: Recording an exemption from personal appearance against an accused makes the memorandum of appearance route unavailable for that accused's pleader.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 33 says every pleader appearing on behalf of an accused who has been exempted from personal appearance shall file a vakkalath as prescribed by rule 32. The instrument and the class of case are both named, so refusing the memorandum route for that accused is the rule and not an inference from it.

requirements.statement: In the High Court, an advocate appearing for an accused in a criminal proceeding MAY file a memorandum of appearance instead of a vakalatnama.
requirements.why: The High Court rules make the memo an alternative on the criminal side, and a great deal of Kerala cheque litigation is at that level in quashing and revision. A system that demands a vakalath from every advocate blocks an appearance the rules expressly allow, and counsel is turned away at the Registry on a requirement that does not apply to him.

binds.target: appearance record - vakalatnama or memorandum of appearance

requirements.how: A memorandum of appearance containing a declaration that the advocate has been duly instructed to appear by or on behalf of the accused.
requirements.test: A High Court criminal appearance can be completed on a memorandum of appearance alone, with no vakalatnama demanded; the same route is not offered on the civil side except for the Government and public servants.
requirements.statusReason: The second proviso to rule 17(1) of the High Court Rules says an advocate appearing for an accused person in a criminal proceeding may, instead of filing a vakalath, file a memorandum of appearance containing a declaration that he has been duly instructed. The permission is express and confined to the criminal side, sub-rule (2) dealing separately with Government and public servants.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record which instrument an advocate's authority to act rests on, as either a vakalatnama or a memorandum of appearance, and MUST NOT default the value.
requirements.why: The two instruments are not interchangeable across courts: a subordinate court pleader appearing for an exempted accused must hold a vakalath, while a High Court criminal advocate may act on a memorandum. The rules prescribe both instruments without saying the record must name which was used, so a system will happily hold neither. If the appearance record does not name the instrument, the court cannot tell whether counsel is authorised to act at all, and the point is taken when an order is challenged for having been made against a party nobody was authorised to represent.

binds.target: appearance record - instrument of authority

requirements.test: Every appearance stores the instrument it rests on and links to that document; an appearance saved with no instrument is rejected, and the value is never populated by default.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 17(1) of the High Court Rules and rule 31 of the Criminal Rules each prescribe an instrument of authority, and rule 33 makes the vakkalath compulsory for an exempted accused in the subordinate courts. Together they mean the two instruments are not interchangeable across courts, but no rule says the appearance record must name which one was used, or forbids a default. That field is our reading of what makes the difference checkable.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT allocate to the Special Court of Judicial Magistrate of the First Class at Kollam any case other than one under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
requirements.why: The notification establishes that court to try cases under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. It confers the designation rather than expressly forbidding other work, so the exclusion is the reading of it. A case-allocation rule that treats the court as an ordinary additional JMFC will route unrelated criminal work to it, defeating the point of the designation and diluting the disposal rate the pilot exists to demonstrate.

binds.target: case allocation to the Kollam Special Court

requirements.test: Attempting to allocate a case of any type other than NI Act s.138 to the Kollam Special Court is refused.
requirements.statusReason: The notification establishes a Special Court of Judicial Magistrate of the First Class to try cases under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. It confers a designation; it does not in terms forbid other work being allocated to that court. Reading the designation as exclusive is the step taken here, and it is why the status is not firm.

requirements.statement: The system MUST hold the Kollam Special Court's Sessions Division and place of sitting as recorded in the notification, and MUST hold the date from which its designation takes effect.
requirements.why: The notification names the Sessions Division of Kollam, the court and the place of sitting, with effect from 20 November 2024. A system that carries the court but not its effective date will show cheque cases instituted before that date as having been within its designation, and a system that carries no division cannot decide whether a complaint filed elsewhere in the division belongs to it.

binds.target: Kollam Special Court - sessions division, place of sitting, effective date

requirements.test: The court record carries the sessions division, the place of sitting and the effective date; a case instituted before that date does not resolve to this court.
requirements.statusReason: The notification names the Sessions Division, the court and the place of sitting by reference to the columns of its Schedule, and gives the designation effect from 20 November 2024. All three particulars, the effective date included, are on the face of the instrument.

requirements.statement: The system MUST hold a court's operating hours as data on the court record, so that a court designated to function round the clock is not constrained by the ordinary sitting hours.
requirements.why: The Kollam court was started as a digital court on a pilot basis as the 24x7 ON Court, against a general rule that courts ordinarily sit from 11.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m. Neither instrument says operating hours are to be held as court-level data; that is what follows from a designated court departing from the general rule. If the sitting window is a constant in the scheduling code, the one court in Kerala designated for cheque cases cannot list a hearing at the hours it was created to work, and the pilot's central feature is unrepresentable.

binds.target: court - operating hours as court-level configuration

requirements.test: The Kollam Special Court record carries a round-the-clock operating window, an ordinary JMFC carries the 11:00 to 17:00 default, and the scheduler reads both from the court record.
requirements.statusReason: The notification starts the Kollam court as a Digital Court on a pilot basis as the 24x7 ON Court, and rule 5(1) says courts shall ordinarily sit from 11.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m. Neither instrument says operating hours are to be held as court-level data; that follows from one designated court departing from the general default. The step is short, but it is ours.

requirements.statement: The system MUST maintain the court diary in the prescribed administrative form, with the entries for a day signed by the Presiding Officer on the day to which they relate.
requirements.why: The diary is signed same-day precisely so it cannot be reconstructed afterwards. A digital diary that lets a Magistrate sign off a week of a cheque case's entries at the end of the month produces a record that is not evidence of what happened on any of those days, and the register the High Court inspects is worthless.

binds.target: court diary - Administrative Form No. 10

requirements.how: Administrative Form No. 10; entries signed by the Presiding Officer on the day to which they relate.
requirements.test: Diary entries carry the date they relate to and the date they were signed; signing an entry on a later date is flagged.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 72(1) requires every court to maintain a diary in Administrative Form No. 10 and says the entries shall be signed by the Presiding Officer on the day to which they relate. The form and the same-day signature are both in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST maintain a hearing book in the prescribed administrative form, distinct from the court diary.
requirements.why: Kerala keeps two records - the diary of the court's day and the hearing book. A system that collapses them into one activity log cannot produce either in the form the rules require, and when a cheque case's history is questioned, neither register exists to answer with.

binds.target: hearing book - Administrative Form No. 11

requirements.how: Administrative Form No. 11.
requirements.test: A day's sittings produce entries in both registers; the hearing book renders in Administrative Form No. 11 and the diary in Administrative Form No. 10, and neither is produced by relabelling the other's entries.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 72(2) requires every court to maintain a hearing book in Administrative Form No. 11, as an obligation separate from the diary in Administrative Form No. 10 in sub-rule (1). The two registers and their two forms are distinguished by the rule itself.

requirements.statement: The system MUST maintain a proceedings paper in the prescribed judicial form recording each judicial step in the case, including the reasons for every adjournment, and MUST record that it was initialled by the Judge or Magistrate in open court.
requirements.why: The rule names the reasons for adjournments first among the steps to be recorded, and in a cheque case the adjournment history is the whole explanation for why a trial the NI Act expects to close in six months has not. A proceedings record that logs 'adjourned' with no reason and no initial cannot answer the delay, and the Kerala field note's picture of files that simply stop moving is invisible in it.

binds.target: proceedings paper - Judicial Form No. 61

requirements.how: Judicial Form No. 61, furnishing full information as to the judicial steps taken - reasons for adjournments, issue of warrants to the accused or witnesses, marking of documents, examination of witnesses, framing of charges, questioning of the accused, hearing arguments and pronouncing judgment or order - initialled by the Judge or Magistrate in open court.
requirements.test: Every adjournment entry requires a recorded reason, and each proceedings paper entry stores the initialling judicial officer.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 73(1) requires a proceedings paper on Judicial Form No. 61 furnishing full information as to the several judicial steps taken, and lists reasons for adjournments first among them; it also requires the entries to be initialled by the Judge or Magistrate in open court. Both the adjournment reason and the initialling are express. The Kerala field note is cited for what such a record would make visible, not as authority for keeping it.

requirements.statement: When the record is sent to a court of appeal or revision, or forwarded on transfer, the system MUST place a typed or neatly written copy of the proceedings paper with the records.
requirements.why: The appellate court reading a cheque appeal needs the running history of the trial, and the original proceedings paper stays with the trial court. If the transmitted bundle carries only the judgment and the exhibits, the Sessions Court cannot see the adjournment history or when the accused was questioned, and remits the case for a record that should have travelled with it.

binds.target: transmission of records - copy of the proceedings paper

requirements.how: A typed or neatly written copy of the proceedings paper placed with the records.
requirements.test: Generating a record bundle for appeal, revision or transfer includes a proceedings paper copy; a bundle without one is blocked.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 73(2) says that when records are sent up to a court of appeal or revision, or forwarded to a court to which the case is transferred or committed, a typed or neatly written copy of the proceedings paper shall be placed with the records. The occasion and the document are both named.

requirements.statement: The system MUST store electronically filed pleadings and documents on a server under the control and supervision of the courts.
requirements.why: The rule places custody with the courts, not with a filing vendor or a general-purpose cloud account. A cheque case file holds the cheque image, the parties' addresses and their bank details, and if it sits on infrastructure the court does not control, the court cannot answer for its integrity or for who has read it.

binds.target: e-filing store - custody and control

requirements.how: An exclusive server under the control and supervision of the courts.
requirements.test: The document store's ownership and access policy resolve to the court, and access to a case's documents is governed by the rules rather than by the hosting provider.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 15(1) requires electronically filed pleadings and documents to be stored on an exclusive server under the control and supervision of the courts, and rule 15(3) puts their security on the courts and makes access a matter for the Rules. Custody with the court is stated, not derived.

requirements.statement: The system MUST label and encrypt each electronically filed case separately, so that it can be identified and retrieved on its own.
requirements.why: Per-case encryption is what stops a single credential from opening every cheque file in the district. It is also what makes retrieval possible when the accused applies for a copy of the record: a store that is encrypted as one volume cannot release one case without exposing the rest.

binds.target: e-filed case - separate labelling and encryption

requirements.how: The Registry shall separately label and encrypt each Action for facilitating identification and retrieval.
requirements.test: Each case's stored documents carry a case-level label and are encrypted with a key scoped to that case; retrieval of one case does not require decrypting another.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 15(2) says the Registry shall separately label and encrypt each Action for facilitating their identification and retrieval. Per-case labelling, per-case encryption and the purpose they serve are all in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST preserve a backup copy of every electronically filed case.
requirements.why: Where the electronic file is the file, its loss is the loss of the case. In a cheque matter the scanned cheque and the bank memo may be the only images of documents whose originals are with a party, and a court that cannot restore them cannot try the case at all.

binds.target: e-filing store - backup

requirements.test: A backup of every case's documents exists, is restorable, and its currency is reportable.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 15(4) says the courts shall take all necessary steps to ensure that a backup copy of all Actions is preserved in the manner decided by the High Court from time to time. The obligation is stated and only the manner is left open, which is why the method carries nothing.

requirements.statement: The system MUST retain the signed vakalatnama, notarised or attested affidavits, and any original document whose authenticity is disputed, for at least three years after the final disposal of the case including any appeal.
requirements.why: The retention clock runs from the end of the appeals, not from the trial court's judgment, and in a cheque case the appeal and a further revision can add years. A retention policy keyed to the date of judgment will destroy the disputed cheque and the affidavit of evidence while the case is still alive on the criminal side of the High Court.

binds.target: document retention - clock from final disposal including appeals

requirements.how: Preserved at least for three years after the final disposal of the Action including appeals, if any.
requirements.test: A case with a pending appeal shows no document as eligible for destruction; the three-year clock starts only when the last appeal is disposed of.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 8(2) requires the signed vakalath, notarised or attested affidavits and any original document whose authenticity is disputed to be preserved at least for three years after the final disposal of the Action including appeals if any. The class of documents, the period and the event the clock runs from are all in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST capture, on an application for a copy, the applicant's name, his position in the proceedings if any, the name of his pleader if any, and a description of the proceeding or document of which a copy is required.
requirements.why: A copy application that does not describe the document cannot be worked, and Kerala returns it. In a cheque case the accused typically wants the complaint, the affidavit of evidence or the deposition of a particular witness, and an application that just says 'case papers' comes back to the applicant after days in the copy queue.

binds.target: copy application - particulars

requirements.how: Presented by the applicant or his pleader, setting out the name of the applicant, his position in the proceedings, the name of his pleader and a description of the proceeding or document of which a copy is required.
requirements.test: The copy application form requires each particular and identifies the target document by reference rather than free text.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 222 requires every application for a copy to be presented by the applicant or his pleader and to set out the name of the applicant, his position in the proceedings if any, the name of his pleader if any, and a description of the proceeding or document of which a copy is required; rule 128(1) of the High Court Rules asks for the same in Form No. 9. The particulars are enumerated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST return a defective copy application for representation after rectification within a period not exceeding seven days.
requirements.why: Kerala caps the time at seven days, and the cap is what stops a copy application from being held indefinitely at the copying section. A return with no deadline, or with a deadline the office sets at will, reproduces on the copy side the file-holding the Kerala field note reports at scrutiny, and the accused's appeal time runs while he waits for the certified judgment.

binds.target: returned copy application - representation deadline

requirements.how: Returned for being represented after rectifying the defects within a period not exceeding seven days.
requirements.test: A returned copy application carries a representation deadline that cannot be set beyond seven days from the return.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 223 says an application not complying with the rules shall be returned for being represented after rectifying the defects within a period not exceeding seven days, and rule 228 repeats the seven-day limit and makes an application not re-presented within it liable to be struck off. The cap is a number in the rule. The Kerala field note is cited for the analogous holding of files at scrutiny, not as authority for the cap.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require an application for an urgent copy to be a separate application setting forth the grounds of urgency.
requirements.why: Urgency in a cheque case is usually the appeal period running against a convicted accused, and Kerala makes him say so in a separate application. A single application form with an urgency toggle lets every applicant claim priority, and the copying section loses the ordering the rules give it.

binds.target: urgent copy application - separate application and grounds

requirements.how: By a separate urgent application setting forth the grounds of urgency; copies are otherwise prepared in the serial order of application.
requirements.test: An urgent copy is applied for on its own application that cannot be submitted without stated grounds of urgency.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 224 says applications for urgent copies shall be by a separate urgent application setting forth the grounds of urgency, and rule 232 makes the ordinary preparation of copies follow the serial order of application except where such an application has been filed and allowed. The separate application, the grounds and the ordering it displaces are all express.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT issue a copy of any proceeding or document other than a judgment to a person who is a stranger to the proceeding, except on an order of the court made on a duly verified petition setting forth the purpose for which the copy is required.
requirements.why: A cheque case file carries the parties' bank particulars, addresses and the cheque image itself. Kerala opens judgments to anyone and everything else only by judicial order on a verified petition. A copy service that treats the whole record as public will release a scanned cheque, complete with account number and signature, to whoever asks for it.

binds.target: copies to a stranger to the proceeding

requirements.how: Allowed only by order of the court obtained on a petition duly verified setting forth the purpose for which the copy is required; judgments are excepted.
requirements.test: A non-party can obtain a judgment; any other document requires a recorded court order made on a verified petition stating the purpose.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 226 says that except in the case of judgments, applications by a stranger to the proceeding for copies of any proceeding or document shall be allowed only by order of the court obtained on a petition duly verified setting forth the purpose for which the copy is required; rule 129 of the High Court Rules is to the same effect and adds that copies of judgments and decrees can be granted to anyone paying the prescribed fees. The exception for judgments and the order requirement for everything else are both stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST have every copy furnished by the court certified to be a true copy by the Head Clerk or the officer appointed for the purpose, and sealed with the seal of the court.
requirements.why: A certified copy of the judgment is what an appeal in a cheque case must be accompanied by, and an uncertified or unsealed print is not one. If the copy the system issues carries no certifying officer and no seal, the appellate registry returns the appeal and the appellant loses the days it takes to get a proper copy.

binds.target: certified copy - certification and seal

requirements.how: Certified to be a true copy by the Head Clerk or officer appointed for the purpose and sealed with the seal of the court.
requirements.test: Every issued copy names the certifying officer and bears the court seal; a copy issued without either is not producible as a certified copy.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 239 requires all copies furnished by the court to be certified to be true copies by the Head Clerk or officer appointed for the purpose and to be sealed with the seal of the court; rule 143 of the High Court Rules requires the same there. Certification and seal are both in the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST endorse on every copy the particulars the rules enumerate, including the dates on which stamp papers were called for and produced, the date the copy was made ready, the date notified for its receipt and the date of delivery.
requirements.why: These dates are how the time taken for obtaining a copy is excluded when limitation for an appeal is computed. A certified copy of a cheque conviction that shows only the date of delivery leaves the appellant unable to prove the exclusion, and an appeal that was in time is dismissed as barred.

binds.target: certified copy - endorsement particulars

requirements.how: Court, year and number of the case, applicant, number and date of application, dates of calling for and producing stamp papers and additional stamp papers, date the copy was made ready, date notified for appearance to receive it, and date of delivery, initialled by the Head Clerk or officer appointed.
requirements.test: The issued copy's endorsement carries every enumerated particular from stored fields, and the appeal limitation calculation can consume them.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 240 enumerates the particulars the endorsement on every copy shall show, among them the dates of calling for and producing stamp papers and additional stamp papers, the date the copy was made ready, the date notified for appearance to receive it and the date of delivery, and requires the endorsement to be initialled by the Head Clerk or other officer appointed. Rule 144 of the High Court Rules imposes the same endorsement, though the list it introduces is not carried in the text held here, so the enumeration relied on is rule 240's.

requirements.statement: The system MUST fix and notify a date for the applicant to receive a copy, and where the copy is not ready on that date MUST fix and notify another on or before the date originally fixed.
requirements.why: The applicant is expected to attend on the notified date, and Kerala requires the court to move the date in advance rather than leave him to discover on arrival that the copy is not ready. A copy workflow with no notified date, or one that re-notifies after the date has passed, wastes the applicant's attendance and stretches the period he can claim to exclude from his appeal time.

binds.target: certified copy - notified delivery date

requirements.how: The Head Clerk fixes a date for the appearance of the applicant to receive the copy and notifies it on the notice board of the court or his section; if the copy is not ready, he fixes and notifies another day on or before the date originally fixed.
requirements.test: Every copy application carries a notified delivery date; re-notification is only permitted on or before the current date, and each notification is stored.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 241 requires the Head Clerk to fix a date for the appearance of the applicant to receive the copy and to notify it, and, if the copy is not ready for delivery on that date, to fix another day and notify it on or before the date originally fixed. Notifying in advance rather than after the event is the sentence's own point.

requirements.statement: The High Court copy workflow MUST refuse a copy of a document forming part of a subordinate court's record except on the order of the Deputy Registrar, obtained on a duly verified petition stating why the copy was not obtained from the lower court.
requirements.why: A quashing or revision petitioner in a cheque case will ask the High Court for copies of the trial court's papers because it is quicker. Kerala requires him to explain why he did not go to the court that holds them. A copy service that supplies them freely pulls the subordinate court's record into the High Court copy queue and loses the endorsement history that the trial court's own copy would have carried.

binds.target: High Court copies of subordinate court documents

requirements.how: Granted only on the orders of the Deputy Registrar obtained on a duly verified petition setting forth the necessity for the copy and the reason why it was not obtained from the lower court.
requirements.test: A copy request against a subordinate court document filed in the High Court requires a recorded Deputy Registrar order and a petition stating the reason.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 130 of the High Court Rules says copies of documents which form part of the records of the subordinate courts shall be granted only on the orders of the Deputy Registrar obtained on a duly verified petition setting forth the necessity for the copy and the reason why it was not obtained from the lower court. The officer, the petition and the two things it must state are all named.

requirements.statement: The system MUST head a memorandum of criminal appeal or a revision petition with a cause title setting out the provision of law under which it is preferred, the name of the court, the names of the appellants and respondents, and the full cause title of the case in the lower court.
requirements.why: Without the lower court cause title the appellate registry cannot tie the appeal to the trial record it has to call for, and a cheque appeal sits unnumbered while the office writes to the trial court to identify the case. Naming the provision matters too: an appeal filed under the wrong provision is returned rather than converted.

binds.target: memorandum of appeal or revision - cause title

requirements.how: A cause title setting out the provisions of law under which it is preferred, the name of the Court, the names of the appellants and respondents in the Court of appeal, and the full cause title of the case or matter in the lower Court or Courts; the same applies so far as may be to revision petitions.
requirements.test: The generated memorandum carries the provision of law, the court, both sets of party names and the full lower court cause title, drawn from the linked trial case record.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 100(1) requires every memorandum of criminal appeal to be headed with a cause title setting out the provisions of law under which it is preferred, the name of the court, the names of the appellants and respondents in the court of appeal and the full cause title of the case in the lower court; rule 100(3) applies the same to revision petitions so far as may be. Each element is enumerated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a memorandum of appeal or a revision petition to be accompanied by a certified copy of the judgment or order appealed against or sought to be revised.
requirements.why: An appeal against a s.138 conviction cannot be numbered without the certified copy, and obtaining it is itself a queue. A system that accepts an appeal on an uploaded uncertified print gives the appellant a false filing, and the return arrives after the thirty days for appealing have run.

binds.target: appeal or revision - certified copy enclosure

requirements.test: An appeal or revision cannot be submitted without a document recorded as a certified copy of the impugned judgment or order.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 102 says every memorandum of appeal or revision petition shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the judgment or order of the court appealed against or sought to be revised. The enclosure is stated as a condition of the filing.
requirements.tightens_hint: the national right of an accused convicted under NI Act s.138 to appeal, and the conditions on which an appeal is entertained

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a memorandum of appeal or a revision petition, where a pleader is engaged, to be accompanied by a duly signed vakalatnama or memorandum of appearance.
requirements.why: The appellate court will not act on a memorandum filed by counsel with no authority on record. In a cheque appeal filed at the end of the thirty days, a missing vakalath is a defect that sends the whole appeal back, and the delay petition it then needs is a further hurdle the appellant did not have to face.

binds.target: appeal or revision - authority of the pleader

requirements.test: Where a pleader is named on an appeal or revision, submission requires an attached signed vakalatnama or memorandum of appearance.
requirements.statusReason: The same sentence of rule 102 requires a vakkalath or memo of appearance duly signed where a pleader is engaged. The condition and the circumstance that triggers it are both in the rule.

requirements.statement: Where an appeal or revision petition is presented after the prescribed period of limitation, the system MUST require a petition to excuse the delay, supported by an affidavit explaining the circumstances, to be filed along with it.
requirements.why: Kerala requires the delay petition to travel with the appeal, not to follow it. An appellate registry receiving a late cheque appeal on its own will return it, and by the time the delay petition is drafted the appellant has added further delay to the delay he has to explain.

binds.target: out of time appeal or revision - delay petition

requirements.how: A petition to excuse the delay supported by an affidavit explaining the circumstances of the delay, filed along with the appeal or revision petition.
requirements.test: Where the computed presentation date is past the limitation period, submission requires an attached delay petition and a supporting affidavit.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 103 says that where an appeal or revision petition is not presented within the prescribed period of limitation, a petition to excuse the delay supported by an affidavit explaining the circumstances of the delay shall be filed along with the appeal or revision petition. That the delay petition travels with the appeal rather than after it is the rule's own words.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a petition or appeal re-presented after the time allowed on its return to be accompanied by a petition to excuse the delay, supported by an affidavit explaining it.
requirements.why: The return of a defective appeal starts its own clock, and Kerala treats a late re-presentation as a fresh delay to be excused. A system that records the return without the allowed time, or that accepts a re-presentation silently whenever it arrives, hides a defect that the registry will raise at scrutiny and that the appellant can no longer explain from memory.

binds.target: late re-presentation - delay petition

requirements.how: A petition to excuse the delay supported by an affidavit explaining the delay, filed with the re-presentation.
requirements.test: A re-presentation after the recorded representation deadline requires an attached delay petition and affidavit before it can be accepted.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 105 says every petition or appeal re-presented after the expiry of the time allowed by the preceding rule shall be accompanied by a petition to excuse the delay supported by an affidavit explaining it, and rule 104 is what fixes that time on the return. The two rules together state the requirement in terms.

requirements.statement: Where a criminal appeal or revision is remanded, re-admitted or transferred from one court to another, the system MUST compute its period of pendency from the date of its original institution.
requirements.why: Kerala fixes the date so that pendency cannot be reset by a procedural event. A system that restarts the clock on transfer will report a cheque appeal that has been alive for three years as newly instituted, and the delay disappears from every statement the court sends up.

binds.target: pendency computation on remand, re-admission or transfer

requirements.how: The date for the purpose of calculating the period of pendency shall be the date of original institution.
requirements.test: Remand, re-admission or transfer of an appeal leaves its pendency computed from the original institution date, and the age reported does not fall.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 140 says that when a criminal appeal or revision case is remanded, re-admitted or transferred from one court to another, the date for the purpose of calculating its period of pendency shall be the date of original institution. All three events and the date are named.

requirements.statement: Where no period of limitation is prescribed by any other law, the system MUST require a revision petition to the High Court to be presented within ninety days of the order complained of.
requirements.why: This is the High Court's residual rule, and it is what applies to the interlocutory orders in a cheque case for which no other period is fixed. A system with no default period will let a revision be filed years after the order and numbered without objection, and the point surfaces only when the respondent takes it at admission.

binds.target: revision petition - residual ninety day period

requirements.how: Ninety days of the order complained of, the provisions of sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applying.
requirements.test: A revision petition against an order for which no other law prescribes a period is flagged out of time beyond ninety days, computed with the benefit of sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 44 of the High Court Rules says that where no period of limitation is prescribed by any other law a revision petition shall be presented within ninety days of the order complained of, and that sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply to such petitions. The residual character of the period, its length and the sections that soften it are all stated.

requirements.statement: The system MUST assemble, with a revision petition to the High Court, the full set of enclosures the rules require, including certified copies of the order sought to be revised and of the judgments below, an additional typed set, an authenticated copy for each respondent, two further copies for the court, and the prescribed service fees.
requirements.why: A revision against a s.138 conviction is returned for any one of these being short, and the enclosure list is long enough that it is routinely got wrong. A filing screen that checks only for the impugned order lets an incomplete revision through, and the Registrar's return costs the petitioner the fifteen days he then has to re-present within.

binds.target: revision petition - enclosure set

requirements.how: Certified copy of the order or decree sought to be revised, certified copy of the judgment on which it is based, certified copy of the judgment or order of the court of first instance, one additional typewritten or printed set of those judgments and orders, as many authenticated copies of the revision petition as there are respondents, two additional copies for the use of the court, and the prescribed fees for service of notice.
requirements.test: The revision filing checklist enumerates every item, scales the respondent copies with the number of respondents, and blocks submission until each is attached.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 45 of the High Court Rules enumerates what a revision petition shall be accompanied by: the certified copies of the order sought to be revised and of the judgments below, one additional typewritten or printed set of them, as many authenticated copies of the petition as there are respondents, two further copies for the use of the court, and the prescribed fees for service of notice. The requirement is that list.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a petition to quash filed under the High Court's inherent jurisdiction to be accompanied by a copy of the proceeding it is directed against, certified as true by the petitioner's advocate or by the petitioner appearing in person.
requirements.why: A large share of Kerala cheque litigation is the petition to quash the complaint, and the rule expressly counts a complaint as a proceeding for this purpose. Without the certified copy of the complaint the High Court cannot see what it is being asked to quash, and the petition is returned at the Registrar's stage before any judge reads it.

binds.target: quashing petition - certified copy of the complaint

requirements.how: A copy of the proceeding against which the petition is directed, certified as true by the advocate of the petitioner or by the petitioner when the petition is filed in person; proceeding includes a complaint.
requirements.test: A quashing petition against a s.138 complaint cannot be submitted without an attached copy of the complaint recorded as certified true by the advocate or the party in person.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 45A says all petitions under section 482 of the Code shall be accompanied by a copy of the proceeding against which the petition is directed, certified as true by the advocate of the petitioner or by the petitioner when the petition is filed in person, and its Explanation says the expression proceeding includes a complaint. That it reaches a section 138 complaint comes from the rule's own Explanation.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record, on the Registrar's return of an insufficiently stamped or defective presentation, a re-presentation period that does not exceed fifteen days.
requirements.why: Fifteen days is the outer limit the Registrar may allow, and a return that names no period leaves the petitioner guessing while the period runs. In a cheque revision that has already been filed near the end of its limitation, a re-presentation a day beyond the allowed time turns a curable defect into a delay that has to be excused on affidavit.

binds.target: Registrar's return - re-presentation period

requirements.how: To be re-presented within a period not exceeding 15 days after supplying the deficiency, curing the defect or making the amendment.
requirements.test: A Registrar's return records a re-presentation deadline that cannot be set more than fifteen days out, and a re-presentation after it is flagged for a delay petition.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 15(2) of the High Court Rules empowers the Registrar to return a memorandum of appeal, petition or other proceeding that is insufficiently stamped, undervalued or defective, for re-presentation within a period not exceeding fifteen days. The cap sits on the face of the power, so a return recording a longer period is outside it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record that a proceeding presented to the High Court was presented in person by the party, his advocate or the advocate's registered clerk, and MUST NOT accept one received by post or telegram unless the court has otherwise ordered.
requirements.why: Kerala's High Court rules exclude postal presentation outright. A revision or quashing petition in a cheque case that arrives by post is not presented at all, and if the software records it as filed, the petitioner is relying on a date the Registry will not accept when the objection is finally raised.

binds.target: High Court presentation - presenter and mode

requirements.how: Presented in person by the party, his advocate or the advocate's registered clerk.
requirements.test: Every High Court presentation names the presenter and their capacity from the permitted set; a postal or telegraphic receipt cannot be recorded as a presentation without a recorded court order.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 32 of the High Court Rules says all petitions, appeals and other proceedings shall be presented in person by the party or his advocate or the advocate's registered clerk, and rule 33 says that unless the court otherwise orders no document sent by post or by telegram shall be received or filed. The permitted presenters and the exclusion of post are both express.

requirements.statement: The system MUST return for rectification any paper presented to the High Court that is couched in improper language, illegible or unnecessarily prolix, treating a paper written in pencil as illegible unless it is an original received by the party.
requirements.why: The rule gives the Registry an express ground of return that has nothing to do with the merits, and it is used. A quashing petition in a cheque case drafted in intemperate terms about the complainant, or a scanned pencil annexure, will come back, and a system that has no way to record this ground of return will log it as an unexplained delay.

binds.target: High Court scrutiny - return for improper language or illegibility

requirements.how: Papers written in pencil are deemed illegible unless they are the originals received by the party.
requirements.test: Improper language, illegibility and prolixity are available as recorded grounds of return, and a returned paper carries the ground it was returned on.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 50 of the High Court Rules says all papers which are couched in improper language or are illegible or are unnecessarily prolix shall be returned for rectification, and its Explanation deems papers written in pencil illegible unless they are the originals received by the party. The three grounds and the pencil rule are the rule's own.

requirements.statement: The system MUST direct a warrant for the levy of a fine by attachment and sale to a Police Officer, in the form the Code prescribes.
requirements.why: The fine and the compensation in a cheque conviction are recovered on this warrant, and it must be directed to a police officer in the prescribed form. A warrant generated to the court's own process server, or on a locally drafted form, will not be executed, and the complainant who has waited through the trial recovers nothing.

binds.target: warrant for levy of fine - addressee and form

requirements.how: Directed to a Police Officer and in Form No. 43 of Schedule II to the Code.
requirements.test: The generated levy warrant names a police officer as the executing authority and cites the prescribed form.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 190(1) says a warrant for the levy of a fine by attachment and sale under section 421(1)(a) of the Code shall be directed to a Police Officer and shall be in Form No. 43 of Schedule II to the Code. The addressee and the form are both named.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record, on a warrant for the levy of a fine, the time limit specified by the issuing authority for the sale of the attached property and for the return of the warrant.
requirements.why: Without a specified return date the warrant has no deadline and nothing brings it back to the court. In a cheque case the compensation cannot be paid out until the levy is accounted for, so an open-ended warrant leaves the complainant's money in limbo and the case shown as disposed while the recovery is unresolved.

binds.target: levy warrant - time limit for sale and return

requirements.test: A levy warrant cannot be issued without a specified sale and return date, and an overdue warrant is reportable.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 190(2) says the authority issuing the warrant shall specify a time limit for the sale of the attached property and for the return of the warrant. Both limits are required by the sub-rule, and specifying them is part of the act of issuing the warrant.

requirements.statement: Where a claim is preferred to property attached under a levy warrant within one month of the attachment, the system MUST record a summary enquiry and a decision with reasons, communicated forthwith to the executing police officer.
requirements.why: A third party claiming the attached property stops the sale, and Kerala gives the claim a one-month window, a summary enquiry and a final reasoned decision. A system with no claim workflow leaves the police officer selling property the court has been asked to release, and the reversal of that sale is a far worse problem than the delay of deciding the claim.

binds.target: claim to attached property - summary enquiry and decision

requirements.how: Preferred within one month of the date of attachment, enquired into summarily, decided with reasons recorded, the decision being final and communicated forthwith to the police officer executing the warrant.
requirements.test: A claim recorded within one month of attachment blocks the sale, requires a reasoned decision, and on decision despatches it to the executing officer.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 190(9) gives a person other than the offender one month from the date of attachment to prefer a claim, and rule 190(12) requires the enquiry to be summary, the decision to be recorded with reasons, and the decision, which is final, to be communicated forthwith to the police officer executing the warrant. The window, the enquiry, the reasons and the communication are all in the sub-rules.

requirements.statement: The system MUST maintain the account of fines imposed, levied and refunded in the prescribed administrative form.
requirements.why: The fine register is the court's cash record, and in a cheque case the fine and the compensation out of it are the substance of the relief. If the system tracks a sentence but not the register, nobody can reconcile what was imposed against what was collected, and a fine recorded as paid in the case file may never have reached the treasury.

binds.target: register of fines - Administrative Form No. 20

requirements.how: Administrative Form No. 20.
requirements.test: The fine register is generable in the prescribed form and reconciles to the sentence and receipt records of each case.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 191 says the account of fine imposed, levied and refunded shall be kept in Administrative Form No. 20. The register and its form are the rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST include, in an order for payment of compensation to the treasury, a certificate in one of the three forms the rules prescribe as to the appeal and revision position.
requirements.why: The Treasury Officer pays on the certificate, not on the judgment. If the payment order carries no certificate, or one that does not match the actual position - unappealable, confirmed on appeal, or the appeal time expired with no appeal - the treasury refuses payment and the complainant makes a second round of the court for a document that should have been right the first time.

binds.target: compensation payment order - certificate

requirements.how: One of: the sentence and award are not subject to appeal or have been confirmed on appeal and no revisional order modifying or reversing the compensation has been received; or the payment order conforms to a modification made in appeal or revision; or the appeal time has expired, no appeal has been preferred and no revisional order has been received.
requirements.test: The generated payment order carries exactly one of the three certificates, selected from the case's recorded appeal and revision history rather than chosen by hand.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 200(1) requires the payment order issued to the treasury to carry a certificate in one of three alternatives: that the sentence and award are not subject to appeal or have been confirmed with no revisional order received, that the payment order conforms to a modification made in appeal or revision, or that the appeal time has expired with no appeal preferred and no revisional order received. Rule 201 supplies the appellate court's certificate where the trial court cannot say whether an appeal was preferred. The three forms are enumerated in the sub-rule.

requirements.statement: The system MUST hold compensation awarded out of a fine as an amount retained in deposit in the treasury, payable to the party only against a payment order issued by the court, and MUST NOT show it as paid to the complainant before that.
requirements.why: Money awarded, money in the treasury and money in the complainant's hands are three different states, and Kerala keeps them distinct through the fine register and the payment order. A case view that collapses them will tell a cheque complainant his compensation has been paid when it is sitting in deposit, and he will not apply for the payment order that is the only way to get it.

binds.target: compensation - awarded, in deposit and paid as distinct states

requirements.how: Retained in deposit in the treasury subject to the order of the court awarding compensation or of the court of appeal or revision, and paid to the party on production before the Treasury Officer of a payment order issued under Rule 200.
requirements.test: The compensation record moves through awarded, in deposit and paid as separate states, and the paid state can only be reached from a recorded payment order.
requirements.statusReason: Rule 203(2) requires the amount to be retained in deposit in the treasury subject to the order of the court awarding compensation or of the court of appeal or revision, and rule 203(3) says it shall be paid to the party entitled on production before the Treasury Officer of a payment order issued under rule 200. Rule 202 carries the same machinery to compensation awarded otherwise than under section 357. Awarded, in deposit and paid are three states the rules themselves keep apart.
